title: PAUL WISHED EVERYONE COULD LIVE LIKE HIM—BUT THEN HE SAID SOMETHING THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: PAUL WISHED EVERYONE COULD LIVE LIKE HIM—BUT THEN HE SAID SOMETHING THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING

What if the life you keep apologizing for is the very place where God wants to reveal His grace? One misunderstood verse about singleness, marriage, desire, and spiritual gifts may finally set someone free from years of unnecessary shame.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that nobody talks about in church.
It is the loneliness of sitting in a room full of people who love Jesus, listening to them celebrate something you desperately wish you had.
Another engagement announcement.
Another wedding invitation.
Another smiling family photograph.
Another well-meaning person asking, “So, when are you getting married?”
You smile.
You laugh.
You say, “In God's perfect time.”
But somewhere underneath that carefully practiced answer is a question you are almost afraid to pray.
“Lord, is there something wrong with me?”
And somewhere else, perhaps in that same church, sits a married person quietly wondering something equally painful.
“Why does everyone make marriage look so easy?”
They love their spouse. They love their children. They believe marriage is a gift from God.
But they are exhausted.
There are bills nobody sees, disagreements nobody hears, disappointments nobody photographs, and nights when two people share the same bed but struggle to understand each other's hearts.
And then there is another person.
Someone who genuinely loves Jesus but does not feel called to marriage.
They are content.
They are growing.
They are serving.
Yet people keep treating their singleness as a problem that needs fixing.
Three different people.
Three different struggles.
One dangerous assumption.
That a life must look a certain way before God can truly be pleased with it.
Then the apostle Paul speaks.
And if we listen carefully, he does not say what many people think he says.
In 1 Corinthians 7:7, Paul writes:
— 1 Corinthians 7:7, King James Version
Read that again.
Paul wished others could live as he did.
But he immediately acknowledged that God had not given everyone the same gift.
That second sentence changes how we must understand the first.
Because Paul was not declaring that everyone should remain unmarried.
He was not announcing that marriage was spiritually inferior.
He was not telling people that having sexual desires made them less holy.
He was recognizing something the church must never forget.
God does not distribute identical gifts to every believer.
And what God has not required of everyone, we must be careful not to impose on everyone.
The original Greek makes this especially meaningful.
Paul begins:
“θέλω δὲ πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἶναι ὡς καὶ ἐμαυτόν”
Thelō de pantas anthrōpous einai hōs kai emauton.
Literally, the sense is:
“But I wish all people to be as I myself am.”
Then comes the crucial qualification:
“ἀλλὰ ἕκαστος ἴδιον ἔχει χάρισμα ἐκ θεοῦ”
Alla hekastos idion echei charisma ek Theou.
“But each one has his own gift from God.”
The word χάρισμα (charisma) means a gracious gift, something given through grace.
It is related to χάρις (charis), the Greek word for grace.
That connection matters.
Paul did not describe his condition as a spiritual trophy he had earned through extraordinary self-control.
He spoke of a gift.
Something received from God.
Not a medal.
Not a ranking.
Not proof that he was more valuable than the married believer sitting beside him.
A gift.
And gifts are not grounds for boasting.
They are reasons for gratitude.
Imagine receiving a beautiful gift from someone who loves you, then turning around and humiliating another person because their gift looks different.
That would be absurd.
Yet sometimes, without realizing it, Christians do something similar.
We elevate one legitimate calling until people with another calling begin to feel spiritually defective.
We make marriage sound like the final evidence of adulthood.
Or we make singleness sound like the ultimate evidence of devotion.
We celebrate the family so loudly that the unmarried feel invisible.
Or we praise undivided ministry so enthusiastically that married believers begin wondering whether their responsibilities somehow make them second-class servants of Christ.
But Paul refuses to let us make either mistake.
His words confront both.
And they bring us back to the grace of God.
To understand why Paul said this, we must understand what was happening in Corinth.
The Corinthian church was wrestling with questions about marriage, sexual relations, celibacy, and how Christians should live faithfully in their circumstances.
Some believers were apparently questioning whether abstaining from sexual relations was the more spiritual path, even within marriage.
Paul addressed these concerns directly.
In 1 Corinthians 7:2–5, he affirmed the responsibilities of husbands and wives toward one another, including mutual marital intimacy. He warned against prolonged deprivation without mutual agreement.
That is important.
Paul was not promoting a spirituality that despised marriage or treats marital intimacy as something dirty.
Marriage was God's good creation long before sin entered the world.
Genesis 2:18 records the Lord saying:
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
And Genesis 2:24 describes the covenant union in which a man leaves his father and mother, cleaves to his wife, and they become one flesh.
Jesus Himself affirmed this creation pattern in Matthew 19:4–6.
Marriage is not an embarrassing concession to human weakness.
It is a good institution established by God.
Yet Paul also recognized that remaining unmarried could offer genuine opportunities for undivided service.
Later in the chapter, he explained that an unmarried believer may be able to devote attention to the things of the Lord in ways that differ from someone carrying the responsibilities of marriage.
In 1 Corinthians 7:32–35, his concern was not to shame married Christians but to encourage devotion to Christ without unnecessary distraction.
He even explained that he was speaking for their benefit, not to place a restraint upon them.
And here is where we must be especially careful.
Paul's preference for singleness was real.
But so was his affirmation of marriage.

In 1 Corinthians 7:8–9, he encouraged the unmarried and widows to remain as he was if they could do so. Yet he also said that marriage was appropriate for those who did not have the self-control required to remain unmarried.
In verse 28, he plainly stated that someone who marries has not sinned.

Later, in verse 38, he acknowledged both marriage and remaining unmarried as legitimate choices, while explaining why he considered remaining unmarried advantageous in the circumstances he was addressing.
He did not erase the distinction between the two.
But neither did he make salvation, righteousness, or God's love dependent upon marital status.
That distinction is everything.
A particular calling may offer particular advantages without making the person who receives it more righteous than someone with a different calling.

Paul also spoke about a “present distress” in 1 Corinthians 7:26. Scholars differ on the precise circumstances he had in mind, but the passage clearly shows that his practical counsel was attentive to the pressures believers were facing.
We should not remove his words from that context and turn them into a universal command that every Christian must remain single.
Nor should we use them to pressure unmarried believers into marriage.
The apostle was teaching wisdom, faithfulness, and devotion under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Not competition.
Not shame.
Not a hierarchy of human worth.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else today.
Because you have spent years measuring your life against someone else's.
You watched your friends get married.
You watched them become parents.
You watched them build homes and celebrate anniversaries.
And somewhere along the way, you started interpreting their blessings as evidence of your failure.
You began thinking that because their story had moved into another chapter, yours had somehow stopped.
But listen carefully.
Another person's blessing is not proof that God has abandoned you.
You are not a half-finished human being because you are unmarried.
You are not spiritually incomplete because you have no spouse.
You are not outside God's purpose because your life does not match the expectations of your relatives, your friends, or your church community.
Your deepest identity was never supposed to come from a wedding ring.
It comes from belonging to Jesus Christ.
Colossians 2:10 declares that believers are complete in Him.
That does not mean every longing disappears.
It does not mean singleness never hurts.
It does not mean marriage is unnecessary or that human companionship has no value.
It means Christ is sufficient to reconcile you to God, give you a new identity, and establish your worth before Him.
You do not need to marry to become fully loved by God.
And if you are married, you do not need to escape your marriage to become fully devoted to Him.
Both truths matter.
Because sometimes married Christians hear Paul's words and quietly wonder whether they chose a lesser path.
Perhaps you have looked at missionaries, pastors, evangelists, or unmarried believers who appear free to serve in extraordinary ways.
You see their schedules.
Their opportunities.
Their mobility.
Their ministry.
And you think, “Maybe I could have done more for God if I had never married.”
But consider something.
The spouse you are learning to love patiently is not necessarily an obstacle to your discipleship.
The children you are raising in the instruction of the Lord are not interruptions to your Christian calling.

The forgiveness you extend after a difficult conversation, the sacrifices you make when nobody applauds, the faithfulness you practice when life becomes ordinary—these can all be expressions of obedience to Christ.
Marriage does not automatically produce holiness.
Neither does singleness.
Holiness is not a marital status. It is a life being transformed by the grace of God.
A person can remain unmarried and still be selfish.
A person can marry and still be spiritually distracted.
A person can serve publicly while neglecting private obedience.
And a person can quietly care for a family while displaying extraordinary Christlike love.
The real question is not simply whether you are married or single.
The deeper question is whether you are honoring Jesus in the life you are living.
And that question leads somewhere uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the problem is not our circumstances.
Sometimes it is what we have allowed our circumstances to become.
Singleness can become an excuse for bitterness.
Marriage can become an excuse for spiritual complacency.
Loneliness can become a doorway to destructive choices.
Domestic responsibilities can become a justification for neglecting prayer, Scripture, and fellowship.
And sometimes we become so preoccupied with the life we wish we had that we stop being faithful in the life God has placed before us today.
That is where the Gospel confronts us.
Not to crush us.
But to call us to repentance and restore our attention to Christ.
Maybe you have made marriage an idol.
You have told yourself that you cannot be happy, valuable, or complete until somebody chooses you.
Maybe you have made independence an idol.
You have convinced yourself that nobody should ever be allowed close enough to challenge your selfishness.
Maybe you have made ministry an idol.
You are so determined to accomplish something impressive for God that you have forgotten how to love the people directly in front of you.
Or maybe you have been quietly resenting God because He has not written your story according to your preferred timeline.
Be honest.
Have you been asking God to bless your life?
Or have you been demanding that He make your life look like somebody else's?
That question can hurt.
But sometimes the truth that exposes our hearts is also the truth God uses to lead us toward healing.
And this is why the story cannot end with Paul.
It must lead us to Jesus.
Because the most important unmarried man in the New Testament is not Paul.
It is Jesus Christ.
Our Lord lived without marrying.
Yet nobody who understands the Gospel would call His earthly life incomplete.
He loved perfectly.
He obeyed the Father perfectly.
He served sacrificially.
He welcomed the rejected.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He showed compassion to the broken.
And He went to the cross to save sinners.
His singleness did not diminish His humanity or His mission.
Yet Scripture also presents marriage as a profound picture of Christ's relationship with His church.
In Ephesians 5:25, husbands are commanded to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Then, in Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul connects the mystery of marriage to Christ and the church.
Do you see the beauty?
The unmarried life of Jesus demonstrates that marriage is not required for a fully faithful human life.
And the biblical covenant of marriage can point beyond itself to the sacrificial love of Christ for His people.
Neither truth cancels the other.
Both direct our attention to Him.
Jesus is not merely the example for single people or the model for married people. He is the Savior both desperately need.
Because the unmarried believer sins.
The married believer sins.
The person who longs for marriage sins.
The person who struggles within marriage sins.
And the person who believes they have mastered their desires still needs grace.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
But the story does not stop with human failure.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
There is the heart of everything.
Christ did not wait until we had perfected our relationships.
He did not wait until we had mastered every desire.
He did not wait until our lives looked respectable.
He came for sinners.
He bore sin on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And through repentance and faith in Him, we receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
That is why our message will always return to this truth:
Not because Jesus promises to give every unmarried person a spouse.
Not because He promises to remove every difficulty from marriage.
Not because surrender guarantees a comfortable future.
But because He can redeem sinners, transform hearts, restore what sin has damaged, and teach His people to live faithfully in whatever circumstances they face.
Perhaps you are single and longing for marriage.
You can bring that desire to God without shame.
Pray honestly.
Seek wisdom.
Pursue godly relationships where appropriate.
Do not pretend you have no desire simply because you think that sounds more spiritual.
But do not surrender your convictions just to escape loneliness.
You do not have to compromise your obedience to Christ to prove that you are worthy of love.
Perhaps you are single and genuinely content.
You do not need to apologize for that either.
You can use the opportunities before you to serve Christ, love others, grow in wisdom, and invest in the church.
Your life does not need to be treated as a waiting room for marriage.
Perhaps you are married and struggling.
Do not allow romantic photographs or carefully edited testimonies to convince you that every faithful marriage is effortless.
Love requires patience.
Repentance requires humility.
Reconciliation requires truth.
And where there is serious harm or abuse, seeking safety and appropriate help is not a failure of faith.
God's Word never gives someone permission to use marriage as a cover for cruelty.
Perhaps you are divorced, widowed, abandoned, or carrying grief that other people do not understand.
This passage is not an invitation for others to make simplistic judgments about your story.
Your circumstances deserve biblical wisdom, compassion, and careful attention to the whole counsel of Scripture.
And none of these experiences places you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the person who has made terrible decisions.
There is room for the person who was betrayed.
There is room for the person who has waited longer than expected.
There is room for the person who thought their marriage would last forever.
There is room for the person who has never been chosen romantically.
And there is room for the person who is finally discovering that being loved by Christ is deeper than being admired by people.
But there is something else in Paul's statement that we must not overlook.
He said:
“Every man hath his proper gift of God.”
The Greek word ἴδιον (idion) carries the sense of one's own or particular.
Paul was acknowledging a real distinction between what God had given to different people.
This does not mean every feeling or present circumstance should automatically be labeled a permanent divine calling.
A person may be single now and marry later.
A person may desire marriage while faithfully remaining unmarried.
A person's season may change.
Paul's words do not give us permission to diagnose everyone's future or claim secret knowledge of God's plans.
They teach us to recognize that God distributes gifts according to His wisdom, and that Christians must live faithfully rather than boastfully.
That is deeply liberating.
You do not need to possess someone else's gift to obey God.
You need to be faithful with what He has entrusted to you.
And even that faithfulness is not something we accomplish independently of His grace.
In 1 Corinthians 15:10, Paul declared:
“But by the grace of God I am what I am.”
He went on to describe his labor, yet acknowledged that God's grace was at work with him.
The same apostle who spoke about different gifts understood that everything he had ultimately depended upon grace.
So perhaps the question you need to stop asking is:
“Why didn't God give me their life?”
And the question you need to begin asking is:
“Lord, how can I honor You with the life I have today?”
Not someday.
Not after the wedding.
Not after the divorce papers are resolved.
Not after someone finally notices you.
Not after the children grow older.
Not after the loneliness disappears.
Today.
In your actual circumstances.
With your real responsibilities.
With your unanswered questions.
With your imperfect heart.
With your need for mercy.
Because Jesus does not call us to wait for an ideal life before following Him.
He calls us to follow Him now.
And perhaps that is the truth somebody has been avoiding.
You have been waiting for your circumstances to change before you surrender completely to Christ.
But what if the next act of obedience is already in front of you?
What if it is forgiving someone?
What if it is confessing hidden sin?
What if it is refusing a relationship that would pull you away from biblical convictions?
What if it is seeking counsel for your marriage?
What if it is learning to serve without needing applause?
What if it is opening your Bible again after months of spiritual exhaustion?
What if it is finally admitting to God that you have been angry, jealous, disappointed, or afraid?
You do not need to manufacture spiritual confidence.
You can come honestly.
Jesus already knows what is inside your heart.
And He is not calling you to hide behind religious appearances.
He is calling you to repentance, faith, and a life surrendered to Him.
And if God has carried you through loneliness, marital difficulties, grief, or a season of waiting, consider sharing a piece of your testimony.
Someone reading may need to know they are not the only one learning to trust Christ in a difficult chapter.
There is no shame in asking for prayer.
There is no shame in admitting you are still growing.
And there is no need to disclose anything too personal publicly. God hears the prayers you cannot put into words.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who has silently concluded that their life is a failure because they are not married.
Somewhere else is a married person who believes they have disappointed God because their home is not as peaceful as they imagined.
And somewhere is a believer who is exhausted from trying to meet expectations God never placed upon them.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because biblical truth is worth passing on.
The Gospel is not only for people who already appear to have everything together.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.

And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you to repent, strengthened your faith, or reminded you of the mercy of Christ, there is another meaningful way you can help us continue.
We want to speak about this with biblical clarity.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Your generosity should never be driven by guilt.
It should flow from conviction, wisdom, gratitude, and love for Christ.
Behind every article is an opportunity to help someone encounter biblical truth.
Behind every devotional is a person who may be struggling to pray.
Behind every resource is the possibility that a believer will open Scripture, understand the Gospel more clearly, and take another step in discipleship.
These items are simply a token of appreciation. The heart of the invitation is not merchandise.
It is helping make biblical encouragement and teaching more accessible.
It is standing alongside a ministry that desires to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
These free resources are part of our desire to nourish faith, strengthen biblical understanding, and encourage spiritual maturity.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read Scripture.
Encourage a struggling believer.
A faithful act of love is not measured by its price.
What matters most is that Jesus Christ is honored and His truth is faithfully proclaimed.
Because in the end, this article was never simply about marriage.
And it was never simply about singleness.
It was about grace.
The grace that reminds us we do not all receive the same gifts.
The grace that calls us to stop comparing our stories.
The grace that confronts our idols.
The grace that meets us in disappointment.
The grace that teaches us to love.
The grace that leads us to repentance.
And above all, the grace revealed in Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again so that those who trust in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
Paul wished that others could live as he did.
But he understood that each person had a different gift from God.
So stop using someone else's life as the measuring stick for your own faithfulness.
Stop treating a wedding ring as proof of spiritual success.
Stop treating singleness as evidence of spiritual superiority.
Stop assuming that because your circumstances are different, God's grace has somehow passed you by.
Look to Christ.
Trust His Word.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in obedience.
And let your life—married or unmarried, joyful or grieving, settled or uncertain—become a testimony to the One who is worthy of everything.
You may not have the life you once imagined, but in Jesus Christ, you are not beyond the reach of the grace that can rewrite your story.
